To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
subpatent parasitaemia is common in low transmission areas of Zambia and is associated with recent malaria symptoms, recent antimalarial use, and age.
subpatent malaria was more common in individuals aged 5 20 years, and 27% of those individuals had detectable gameto- cytemia, suggesting that subpatent infections may be a source of transmission.
subpatent malaria was detected in 2.6% of individuals surveyed and 47% of these individuals had subpatent infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the development of the malaria transmission in southern Zambia.
the identification and treatment of asymptomatic, Plamodium infected individuals through the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RTDs).
the identification and characterization of the subpatent malaria parasite reservoir in a pre elimination setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study has shown that the characteristics of the subpatent reservoir of malaria in a pre elimination setting in Southern Zambia.
the characteristics of individuals with sub patent (RDT negative, but PCR positive) Plasmodal parasitemia were examined in southern Zambia, a setting with low levels of transmission.
the findings suggest that strategies for malaria elimination in Zambia will need to target individuals with both patent and subpatent parasitemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in a setting of declining malaria transmission and malaria elimination efforts, individuals with submicroscopic parasitemia are more likely to be asymptomatic, and are less likely to be infected with gametocytes.
subpatent malaria is an important component of the asymptomatic reservoir of malaria in Zambia.
subpatent malaria, as defined by RDT negative and PCR positive, is an important reservoir of malaria in southern Zambia and is associated with asymptomatic infection and asexual parasite densities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the malaria reservoir in a pre-elimination setting consists of both symptomatic and subpatent infections, and the subpatent reservoir is comprised of both asexual and sexual stages.
the malaria parasite can persist at low levels in the human body for long periods of time, even in areas where malaria has been reduced.

in low transmission settings, the majority of individuals with sub-patent parasitemia are asymptomatic, and therefore, strategies based on active case detection are likely to miss this reservoir of infection.
